newsitem.title: USA: Talks continue at two GM parts plants.
newsitem.headline: Talks continue at two GM parts plants.

text.p: Production was expected to resume as normal on Monday at two General Motors Corp. parts plants that had threatened strikes as negotiations for new local labor contracts continued on Sunday.
The United Auto Workers union has extended strike deadlines hour-by-hour at GM's catalytic converter plant in Oak Creek, Wis., and its metal stamping plant in Grand Rapids, Mich.
Strikes at either of the two factories could have a significant impact on GM's North American car and truck production.

The Oak Creek plant, near Milwaukee, employs 870 hourly workers and makes exhaust system catalytic converters for nearly all of GM's North American car and truck models, while the Grand Rapids plant employs 2,346 and stamps out sheet metal parts for a variety of GM vehicles, including its all-new minivans.

Talks continued at both plants on Sunday as the two sides tried to resolve disputes over staffing levels, the shifting of work to outside suppliers and long-term business plans. UAW Local 1866 in Oak Creek had originally set a midnight Thursday deadline, while Local 730 in Grand Rapids had set midnight Friday deadline.

GM reached a tentative agreement late Friday for a new local labor contract at a foundry in Saginaw, Mich., averting a threatened strike by about 900 members of UAW Local 445. The foundry produces pistons, piston rods and transmission parts for a variety of GM vehicles.

The two sides also continued nearly round-the-clock negotiations to end a nearly eight-week-old strike by 5,800 workers at GM's Pontiac, Mich., pickup truck plant. Ron Miller, president of UAW Local 594, said Saturday that GM had made some new proposals to the union in recent days.
"I'm not optimistic that we're close to an immediate settlement," another member of the union bargaining committee said Sunday.

The union struck on April 22 over demands for more jobs to ease an increasing workload. Initial demands by the union called for GM to hire 600 new workers at the full-size pickup truck plant and related truck development facilities.
GM has resisted, saying it needs to reduce its workforce to more competitive levels. A new-generation pickup truck slated to be built in Pontiac and two other plants will require

Until this week, talks at Pontiac and the three parts plants have moved slowly. Some analysts view the multiple strike deadlines as a move by the UAW to increase pressure for GM to settle the Pontiac walkout.

GM, which has been plagued by troublesome local negotiations more than eight months after it reached a national labor pact with the UAW, also has several other unresolved local disputes, including one at a mid-size car plant in Fairfax, Kan.
The world's largest automaker has suffered five local strikes so far this year.
